projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr. was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr. [5/28/2010]

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Well, that's fine too, then you won't leave anything out. Well, like I said, my name is Adrian Poteet and we're here with the Veterans History Project just to take any of your experiences that you want to share with everyone they'll be filed with the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Okay. I appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Okay, lets just start out with can you say your name for the record?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Benjamin Franklin Pace.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: What's your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: March 5th, 1926.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: When were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: I was drafted in 1944 but --

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Where did you grow up? Where did you live at the time?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: I -- I was born in Dallas, the city of Dallas. About probably six or eight blocks from Fair Park right over here in East Dallas.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Okay. Lets see, so, when you joined where did they send you first?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: I went to -- four days, I remember four days it took me to get to -- from Dallas to San Diego on a train.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Mm hmm.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Going out there they pulled us over we on the side -- the side we sat there for two or three, four hours and here come two guys by on the handcar and they got past the train and we pulled right and kept going. It was a real trip. My first trip away from Dallas.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Was it?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: I never had left Dallas.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: In my life.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: So I'm sure you saw lots of things that you --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Oh my, yes, I was scared to death.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Uh-huh, did you join with any friends?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: The way I -- the way I started, really, to start this thing off I told them when they called me that I was one of the young ones. I -- when -- they bombed Pear Harbor I was 15 years old and I -- I didn't go into service until '44 and -- and didn't get into, you know, all of the bad, really bad action for war and I was talking about possibly saying well -- there was people that really did a lot of things for this country and they deserve to be heard and she said well, we want to get a -- a cross section of everybody. Then I remembered talking to my brother, my older brother, and he joined the service in '39 so he was in World War II and Korea -- the full thing. And -- and 1953 when I got out of service I was talking to him and I said, Bud, you've done your duty. You've won 35 medals. And he said, somebody, somebody has to do this. So, he was killed in '54 and he'd be 36 -- so for him and guys like him.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Great, great, we're glad. Lets see --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Yea, so I went to San Diego going through boots found out -- found out right quick how the Navy works. Got there went to bed about two in the morning, 4 o'clock reveille you get up, go to breakfast. I went in and the hot steam of the stainless steel trays, hot so you can't hardly hold them. Going down there -- being served buffet style. Swap! I looked and there was a pile of beans. And moved on down and boom, a piece of corn bread.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: For breakfast?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Move on, that was breakfast. Once a month that's the tradition in the Navy, beans and corn beard.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: And the corn breads more like cake, let me tell you. But that's -- that's another -- I learned, learned a lot of things in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Well, what do you remember about boot camp? How did they prepare you?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Okay. Went in and -- get a haircut, just line up everybody, get in this one -- you know, barking at you, barking. So, {coughing} -- I'm standing behind this fellow from California long, black hair had a zoot suit on. He was dialed out and he was a talker. Well, so this guys giving him a haircut he starts talking and the guy says mm hmm and he just keeps giving him a haircut, mm hmm and he keeps talking, yea, yea and he's cutting his hair off more and more every time, but to start off with he stroked it and he said you like this hair and the guy says yea. He said zip and it fell in his lap and he said there it is. Anyhow, so normally we had a haircut about an inch long. This guy when he finally got out of the chair his hair -- he was like you see walking around now just almost bald. And I learned keep your mouth shut and do what they's tell you. That's -- that was my first lesson and -- but we -- we did we wore out a pair of shoes marching.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Mm hmm.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: On this grinder and had to have them resewn but I had -- had the ROTC in high school.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: So I knew all about marching and manual of arms and all of the things {coughing} -- that they were asking but one thing I didn't know is how to swim, being a city boy not around any swimming pools, so they said before you can get out of boot camp you've got to swim 50 feet. Oh, I looked at that swimming pool, you know, just swim across that pool and back. I can't swim. He said, you know dog paddling everybody can do that. Well, I don't know. He reached over and he had this long fishing pole, bamboo fishing pole.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Mm hmm.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: He said, see this? Tapped the water out there and he says you get in trouble I can give you the pole and pull you in. I said well, okay. So I got back, run, and jumped as far as I could come up dog paddling and got across and I was pretty tuckered and he said well, come on back. And I said can't do it. And he said come on back. He said look I got you. Well, all right. So I get started and I got about halfway -- Whew, give me the pole, give me the pole, I'm going to drown! He -- he got that pole and every time I come up he'd hit me behind the head. He said, get out of there, get on across. So he drove me across with that pole. And I -- I got over to the other side; you made it, you graduated, you can graduate. He said you can get out of the pool and I said I ain't got -- enough energy left. Well, he said well just sit there until you get the energy because I'm not helping you. So I did get out but that I remember. Those are the -- so, you do what they tell you.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Lets see -- so, then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: My next assignment they give you three choices where would you like to go, submarine _____. Well, you go where they tell you to go and I went to -- NATTC, that's a technical training school in Memphis, Tennessee to learn to be a aircraft operator, radio operator. So I went to radio school and radar school. And it was a combat air group -- combat air crew and we -- we had -- we learned Morse code which was prevalent in World War II.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: And -- had to learn radar. Secret, it was a secret and they -- they threatened us said you be -- you could be shot if you divulge any of the information over radar. Well, we'd go into town all the waiters and waitresses they knew more about radar than we did. In fact, somebody was talking but it wasn't me. Then after that, graduated from that, and we had to learn Morse code at 20 words per minute. I had to learn semaphore, always with communication.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Semaphore?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Semaphore, yea. With the flags and -- then after that we went to Gunnery school where we learned to fire the different pieces of equipment they had -- they had .30 caliber, .50 caliber, and the Martin electric current -- gun current -- so we would be conversing at all the different types of -- of equipment that's the -- had my first mishap with a .50 caliber because you had to chin it and hold your chin like this so -- sight and the -- the thing blew up in my face, so I had a blackened face scared but no -- no damage other than.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Probably had to change clothes.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: I'm sure that happened to more than just you.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes, very definitely to me.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Then did you say you ended up being a pilot?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: I -- I went to -- from there I went on -- I -- while I was waiting for the -- to get lined up with my flight crew, my final advance crew, which was going to be PBM'S, flying boats -- Martin PBM's. I crewed as a ground crew, took care of a PV-2 Ventura at -- what was that -- Buford, South Carolina and I was there for about two or three months then I went on to Banana River, Florida while we were at -- at Buford this friend of mine said, say, I know how we can goof off a couple of days so we won't have to work out on this hot line. How's that? We go apply for flight training. And I said I already -- when I was in high school talked to them about that and they said it would take too long. And he said, yea but the fact we can spend two days inside. And I said well, yea, that's -- that will work so we went over and did two -- two days worth. Well, we went back and -- went back and got to looking at the reports as they came out and I went down through that list and on and on and on, finally, May 1952 -- now this was in 1944 -- '45, early '45, 1945. They said you could expect to be called up in May of 1952 that's how far down the list I was. Well, so I went ahead and got lined up with my crew and we were flying practice missions over the Atlantic as part of a combat air crew and we do searchs and things like that and submarine patrols and I got a call one day from the office report -- I said, Man, I got in trouble again. And I went up there and he said pack your clothes. What do you mean? He said you got ten days to get to San Luis Obispo, California. What, what, what? He said, your going into flight training. I said I was -- wasn't scheduled until May of '52. Oh well, they -- combat air crew got bumped to the top of the list and that's you. So, I said, well, I -- I've already got my crew, I don't want it. Tell them I don't want it. You tell them, and said it will be the bureau and the name of personnel Washington, D.C. that said in the meantime, I believe I'd get on that airplane and get gone. So that's why I went into pilot training. I went to San Luis Obispo, California Polytechnic went through an accelerated course to a refreshment -- refresher for two years of college and we -- we hit the highest spot and then I went to Saint Mary's for primary for the officers training -- and nine months of training in primary. I was on the base, didn't leave the base had to walk, didn't -- wasn't near a car for nine months wasn't off the base for nine months. Studying six days a week starting at six and bed check at 10 o'clock, lights out.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: That's hard work.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: That was, yea -- that was -- that -- we were busy. Had -- it was this little small Catholic college and there was -- we kept seeing this Cadillac pull up to the -- the door and a chauffeur jumped out and opened the door. Who in the world is that? It looked like some student. And that's Henry Wedemeyer, the all American. And I said, Oh, Okay. Yea, that was -- he put Saint Mary's on the map. He later become an actor and he was in -- he was a sergeant in Hawaii Five-O.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Oh, Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Yea, that's Herman Wedemeyer. Anyhow, then, lets see. World War II -- the Japanese had surrendered by that time so we were in the 45's and so I continued I graduated from primary so I got -- finally got a 30 day leave and they said you can go home, you got to report to Corpus Christi, Texas and -- Corpus that's the second stage of a flight -- advance. And -- so I went saw all of my friends they all had enough points by then everybody in World War II you accumulated points for discharge according to what you did -- if you were wounded if you were, you know, in combat -- months, so many months service and all of these accumulated and the higher the number the earlier you got out. Well, of course, I had accumulated enough points to get out but I kind of liked the Navy, wish I would have stayed -- but -- I said okay. That'll work but all my buddies we dranking beer and having a good time and partying and all well after 30 days of that living it up going back down there and the first day they busted the door. What are you doing in bed? I said I don't check in until 8 o'clock this morning. Get out of bed. Get out of that bed. I said, uh-oh I remember now. I said I don't know whether I want this or not. So I went down talked to the CO and he says, Oh, with your record we want -- you really -- we want -- we need you to stay. Well, I don't know, you know, and he -- he said take three more days make it out there and then come back Monday and see me. Yes, sir. So he gets me a pass and three more days, shouldn't have done it. Then I said -- come back and I said, yep, want to go home. Besides, really my dad was sick and I need -- I got four younger brothers and sisters and I figured Cadets pay is not very much I was ending up -- I was sending it, a lot went back but I was ending up with -- $15 cash a month to live on and I said, Nah, I better go home take care of my family so I -- I -- they said well stay in the reserve. Okay, I'll sign up for naval reserve, so I did. So, then I went back to the house. That was my World War II experience so I didn't do anything, but a lot of them did a lot but like my brother they did all of it, they did a lot. They're the real heros.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Yea. Do you want to tell us about your brother?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Do you want to tell us about your brother?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Well, yea. He was okay he went in 1940 -- '39, he was down in Randolph Field and he was a mechanic and so he -- he went to all the different mechanics schools and he was an -- on the B-17's he flew in the 8th Air Force in -- in Europe -- and -- when he come back in, lets see, he went into B-29's and of course he was -- he was in the -- of course, stayed in the Air Force and he went on in to -- he was into Korea in -- all through Korea and they were stationed in Okinawa and flew out of Okinawa and went all through that part and -- but the latter part of World War II he did participate some in -- in I believe in -- in -- in Asia, in Southeast Asia, but I can't remember for sure. I got all these records, lets see -- but then that's when I -- in '53 I had transferred over and in 1950 to the Air Force because my friend told me that hey you know we can fly out here at Hensley Field and all we had to do is join the reserve, we can go out there and fly. I said, Oh, that'd be nice and so we did. Well, when the Korean thing come about they said fellow we'll have a meeting so we all met at Woodrow Wilson and the CO got up there and says, don't worry guys they'll never call us up. Well, ten days later, greetings come on in, we need you and we were combat air crew all of us. So then -- so in '53 after I had done my stint in Korea thing I saw my brother and by this time he had transferred from B-29's to B-36's and he was flying out of South Dakota and he said -- he come by one day had some time and he said, Well, they give me orders I may be going to B-52's which is over in Fort Worth.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Mm hmm.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: And I said, Boy that'd be great we'll be able to see you. He said, You'll see me when I put my foot on the porch because things happen, you know. Well, then that's when I talked to him and I said Bud, you've done your share, you know, you've had some tight squeezes. He's been hurt. And he said, somebody has to do it so it might as well be me. And that was the thing that stuck with me from then to now. It really -- special people.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: His attitude?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Yea, yea. Well, lets see, that's he -- he was on a training flight there was 23 men aboard the plane, B-36 and they flew from South Dakota to South America to Africa to England and they were on their way back when they -- these things pusher engines -- I don't know if you know what a B-36 -- but they had -- they had a pusher engine and they had some jettle They called them ?jettle? then -- a jet assist and the -- the engines went out on one side of the plane. The -- the jets went out, the radar went out, and so it was very coincidental and all that. So they were gonna to take a force landing in Newfoundland. {Coughs} When they were going in the -- the plane hit the very top about 50 feet from the top of this little mountain. If it had been 50 feet up or 50 feet even to the left or the right they would have cleared the mountain, but to hit 50 feet slid up and over and killed all aboard. Well, my sister went up to the site about I guess in '73 and she went down to this little village and there was a guy down there mending net and {coughs} excuse me. Mending this net and she asked him if he would know anybody that knew about this site and he smiled and said, I was one of the ones help bring them out.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: So he had brought the bodies out from there. He said, I can take you to it.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: And she said, Well, you know. She's older than me, my sister. And he said, it -- it's just a up a little old hill. Well, them fisherman, Scottish fisherman up there tough as boots and rugged. He took them over there and they made it up this hill and over the top of the hill and there was that airplane. Look like the day it hit.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Didn't deteriorate at all because it was on -- on the east side of the -- of the island so all the moisture wouldn't get to it. And so my brother-in-law brought me back some souvenirs -- souvenirs off that airplane. The people at the village took one of the propellors and made a monument to these guys and it's really nice. They're real good genuine people.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Yea, but that's my brother.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: What -- what is his name?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: James Earl Pace.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Great. Well, is there anything else that you'd like to tell us?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I -- I feel grateful that the Honor Flight group has been given the record mission for World War II Vets and that was my first trip to Washington the trip and I was very, very impressed. Was -- we were the first group to visit Walter Reed Hospital of the Veterans and met about, I imagine, a 100, 150 of these young people up there. Young warriors and they have -- they carried, they're carrying the torch that we had. It's great.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: It's good to see.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Well, I'm -- thank you for giving me the chance to interview you. I'm glad to be a part of this too and -- I guess that's all we have today but we appreciate your time.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I -- I thank you. And like I said, I didn't -- I didn't do much myself but I'm just a part of -- you do what they ask you to do. And I -- I did -- and I did it gladly as all the rest of them did.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Yea, we'd do it again if we weren't so darned old.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: {Laughter} That's very interesting about your brother.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: That's very interesting that your sister got to see -- that your sister got to see the site. Interesting.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Adrianell Poteet
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Franklin Pace, Jr.
sp.p: All right.
